en: The Parivāra:
The Analysis of the Bhikkhunī Rules,
Second Part
2.16 Section on the Compendium (Samuccayavāra) On account of consenting to physical contact, how many offenses does one incur?
On account of consenting to physical contact, one incurs five offenses.
If a lustful bhikkhunī consents to being grasped by a lustful man below the collarbone and above the knees, it is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika).
If a bhikkhu touches body with body, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa);
if he touches what is connected to the body with the body, it is an offense of serious transgression (thullaccaya).
If one touches what is attached to the body with what is attached to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing;
if one tickles with a finger, there is an offense entailing expiation.
On account of consenting to physical contact, one incurs these five offenses.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
By how many of the seven classes of offenses are they comprised?
By how many of the six origins of offenses do they originate?
Of the four kinds of legal issues, which one is it?
By how many of the seven principles for settling disputes are they settled?
Those offenses belong to two of the four failures.
There may be a failure in virtue, and there may be a failure in conduct.
Among the seven classes of offenses, it is comprised within five classes of offenses:

it may be an offense entailing defeat (pārājika), it may be an offense of formal meeting (saṅghādisesa), it may be a grave offense (thullaccaya), it may be an offense requiring expiation (pācittiya), or it may be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from one origin:
they originate from both body and mind, but not from speech.
Of the four legal issues, it is the legal issue of an offense.
Of the seven methods of settling disputes, they are settled by three methods:

there may be settlement by means of both face-to-face resolution (*sammukhāvinaya*) and acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*); there may be settlement by means of both face-to-face resolution and covering over as with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*) … [and so on] … How many offenses does one incur by reason of asking for and eating curd?
By requesting curd and eating it, one incurs two offenses:
if one accepts it with the thought, "I will eat," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);
for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya).
Having requested curd, one incurs these two offenses by reason of eating it.
To how many of the four failures do those offenses belong?
By how many of the seven classes of offenses are they comprised?
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins do they originate?
Of the four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), which legal issue is it?
Of the seven principles for settling disputes (*samatha*), by how many principles for settling are they settled?
Those offenses belong to one of the four failures— namely,
failure in conduct (*ācāra-vipatti*).
Among the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*), they are included in two classes of offenses.
It may be by way of the class of offenses entailing confession (*pāṭidesanīya*), or it may be by way of the class of offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Of the six origins of offenses, they originate from four origins:
they may originate from the body, but not from speech or mind; [and so forth].
There may be [actions] that originate from both body and speech, but not from mind;
there may be those that originate from both body and mind, but not from speech;
and there may be those that originate from body, speech, and mind.
Of the four kinds of legal issues, it is a legal issue arising from an offense.
Of the seven principles for settling disputes, it is settled by three principles:
sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by acting according to what is admitted; sometimes by resolution face-to-face and by covering over as with grass.
The eighth section on combinations is finished.
The eight sections on conditions are finished.
In the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga, the sixteen great sections are finished.
